narrator
paragraphs.text: Where this comes from. This is a simplified and shortened adaptation of a BBC Future article by the technology writer Thomas Germain. He spent a week testing Meta's new AI agent, "Muse". Only a few short phrases are quoted directly; the rest has been rewritten for this course.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Read the original BBC article →

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Last month, Meta released a new AI agent called Muse. An agent is different from a chatbot. A chatbot answers your questions; an agent goes out into the world and does things for you. Muse has its own web browser. It can cancel your gym membership, argue about a price with customer service, order your groceries, and invite your friends to a party. Soon, it will be able to make phone calls, too.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Muse is the first free, full-featured agent from a big technology company, and millions of people downloaded it in the first few weeks. Other companies are building agents as well. To do its job, Muse asks for a great deal of trust: it wants to read your email and your calendar, and on some computers it asks to control the whole machine.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: This sounds convenient. But the experts who spoke to the BBC say it is the start of a difficult period for the internet. The web was designed for humans, who have limited time and patience. AI agents have neither.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In 2024, fans of the singer Taylor Swift found that concert tickets in the United States were extremely expensive. Many of them flew to Europe instead, where the same tickets cost much less. Ticket scalpers — people who buy tickets only to resell them at a higher price — had taken most of the seats before real fans could.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Now imagine that every fan has a personal scalper robot. Calli Schroeder, who works for a privacy group in the United States, predicts that this problem will "explode". When you try to book a table at a popular restaurant, or renew a passport in the busy season, you may find that agents have already taken every slot. Because booking is effortless for a machine, some people will even hoard appointments — booking five "just in case".

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The trouble does not stop at tickets. If one agent sends 600 enquiries to a small business while an ordinary person might send two, the business is buried under machine-made messages. Robots do not look at advertisements and do not buy subscriptions, and many websites depend on exactly that money.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: For years, traffic from bots has quietly grown. One study found that bot traffic rose by more than 120% in the year to June 2026 — roughly nine times faster than traffic from real people. Some websites are already struggling to stay online under the load.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: There are personal risks, too. Schroeder says that if you let an agent plan your holiday, you cannot easily check whether it found the best price — or a flight that pays its own company a fee instead. She examined Muse's terms of service and says they do not promise that the agent will act in your interest.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Security experts also found serious flaws in the Muse app within days of its release. Meta says the problem was fixed immediately, and that Muse had been delayed for months to make it safer. But the researcher who found the flaw said the mistakes were so easy to find that he could not trust the company's promises.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is pessimistic. Ramesh Raskar, a professor at MIT, says we need "rules of the road".

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Raskar suggests treating the AI models as engines and the agents as cars, and then writing real traffic rules for them: windshields, brakes and traffic lights. Some of that is already beginning. A few restaurant booking platforms have banned people who misuse AI. The UK rewrote the rules for booking driving tests, partly to fight bots. And some websites are now testing a "pay-per-crawl" system that charges AI programs a fee when they collect the site's data.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The road ahead will be bumpy, and users will pay a price in personal data. But the internet was rebuilt for smartphones once before — with apps, mobile pages and touch screens. It can be rebuilt for agents, too.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: A note on balance. This article looks mainly at the problems, because that is what the experts were asked about. Meta argues that Muse is safe and that users stay "in charge". Keep both sides in mind when you discuss the questions below.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The article describes one problem with many players. The table shows what each player must, must not and should do — the same grammar you will practise further down the page.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Talk about it. Choose one row. Does everyone in your group agree? Change one cell and explain why your version is better.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: The article is full of rules: what agents should do, what websites must not do, and what is simply not necessary. Here are the modals from the Week 6 lesson, with examples from this article.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Watch out. mustn't (forbidden) and don't have to (not necessary) are not the same. And there is no to after a modal: ✗ I must to go → ✓ I must go.

paragraphs.text: MeaningNot a standard phrase. The writer creates a name (from Taylor Swift's fans) for one kind of damage.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In contextWhen everyone has a robot that books first and asks later, the demand for a limited resource — tickets, tables, appointments — explodes.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Try it: "Cheap bots create a Swiftie problem for anything in short supply."

paragraphs.speaker: narrator

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In contextA business is buried under messages: it receives far more than it can possibly deal with.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Try it: "The team was buried under support tickets after the launch."

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: MeaningTo decide to think about something in a particular way, for a practical purpose.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In contextRaskar says: "treat the models like an engine, and the agents like cars". He sets up a comparison to make his rule-making idea clear.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Try it: "Treat the API as a service, not a product."

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: MeaningThe shared rules that stop people from crashing into each other. Here, used as a metaphor.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In contextThe "road" is the internet, the "cars" are AI agents, and the missing rules are the laws and standards that do not exist yet.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Try it: "Before we ship it, we need rules of the road for who is responsible."

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: MeaningTo suffer a cost or a loss in order to get something.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: In contextUsers get the convenience of agents, but "pay a price" in personal data. A toll also fits the road metaphor.

paragraphs.speaker: narrator
paragraphs.text: Try it: "We saved time, but we paid a price in accuracy."
